title: 2 Kings 6:1–7
context: 2 Kings 6:1–7 records a small miracle among the sons of the prophets. Their meeting place is too small, so they go to the Jordan to cut beams, and Elisha goes with them. An ax head, which was borrowed, falls into the water. Elisha throws a stick where it fell and makes the iron float, and the man takes it. Both traditions read the account as showing God’s care for ordinary needs and for a poor man’s anxiety over a borrowed tool, and they see it as part of the series of Elisha’s miracles that display God’s power in everyday life.

verses.text: The sons of the prophets said to Elisha, “See now, the place where we live and meet with you is too small for us.
verses.arminianNotes: The sons of the prophets tell Elisha that the place where they live and meet with him is too small. Arminian readers see a growing community of prophets in Israel, a sign that God was preserving faithful people even during a time of widespread unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the growth as God’s work in preserving a remnant. Both traditions read the verse as setting a scene of ordinary community life in which God will act.

verses.text: Please let us go to the Jordan, and each man take a beam from there, and let’s make us a place there, where we may live.” He answered, “Go!”
verses.arminianNotes: They ask to go to the Jordan, each cut a beam, and build a place to live, and Elisha tells them to go. Arminians see the community taking practical initiative, and they see Elisha supporting their plan.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see shared work and planning as fitting for God’s people. Both traditions read the verse as part of a simple account that highlights everyday faithfulness and cooperation.

verses.text: One said, “Please be pleased to go with your servants.” He answered, “I will go.”
verses.arminianNotes: One asks Elisha to come with them, and he agrees. Arminian readers see the desire for the prophet’s presence as valuing God’s servant among them, and they see Elisha’s willingness to share in their ordinary work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see Elisha as a humble leader who stays with the community in its daily needs. Both traditions read the verse as preparing for the miracle in which his presence proves important.

verses.text: So he went with them. When they came to the Jordan, they cut down wood.
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha goes with them, and they cut down trees at the Jordan. Arminians read the verse as a simple transition into the account, showing the community at work together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and treat the verse as narrative setting. Both traditions note the Jordan’s earlier role in Elisha’s ministry (2 Kings 2:13–14; 5:14) and read the verse as leading to another display of God’s power there.

verses.text: But as one was cutting down a tree, the ax head fell into the water. Then he cried out and said, “Alas, my master! For it was borrowed.”
verses.arminianNotes: As one man cuts a tree, the ax head falls into the water, and he cries out that it was borrowed. Arminian readers see the distress of a poor man who could not afford to replace a borrowed tool, and they note God’s concern for such ordinary troubles.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that iron tools were valuable at the time. Both traditions read the man’s cry as an honest appeal to Elisha in a real need, the kind of situation in which God shows his care.

verses.text: The man of God asked, “Where did it fall?” He showed him the place. He cut down a stick, threw it in there, and made the iron float.
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha asks where it fell, throws a stick into the water there, and makes the iron float. Arminians see God’s power working in a small, practical matter, showing that no need is too small for his care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the miracle as God’s power over the natural world. Both traditions avoid allegorizing the stick and the iron and read the event as a straightforward sign of God’s care for his people.

verses.text: He said, “Take it.” So he put out his hand and took it.
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha tells him to take it, and he reaches out and takes it. Arminian readers see the man’s simple response of reaching out as completing the miracle, which restores what was lost.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and read the verse as a quiet conclusion. Both traditions see the account as showing God’s care for ordinary needs, which encourages his people to bring every concern to him.
